problem: Robots have no awareness of how loud their own actions (motors, speakers) will be at a listener's location. Distance-only heuristics ignore walls, corridors, and materials, and existing audio-for-robotics work focuses on localizing external sound sources rather than self-generated noise.
motivation: Home robots such as vacuums and quadrupeds can be very loud, and the only current remedy is a 'do not disturb' mode that stops the robot. Sound loudness depends on geometry and materials, so a robot that perceives its surroundings visually could estimate the noise it makes at a listener and plan quieter paths without stopping.
key_idea: Train a visual Acoustic Noise Predictor on SoundSpaces impulse-response simulations that maps a robot-centric panorama plus the listener's relative distance and direction to the max dB at the listener, then use it as a noise cost in A* planning alongside time.
insight: Visual context adds information beyond distance: the panoramic VisDirDis model covers the true data distribution best and has the best epsilon-accuracy, while the distance heuristic, DisLinReg and DirDisMLP are unimodal or too narrow. Ablations show the panorama beats the ego-centric 90° view, which misses high-dB outliers at long range. Classification with 16/64/128 bins trains faster and captures outliers but gives coarser granularity. The sim-to-real study is a negative result: the model largely relies on distance and fails to capture walls or corridors in real panoramas.
method: Data generation: sample robot (source) and listener locations (within 10 m) in Matterport3D via Habitat and SoundSpaces 2.0, simulate the RIR, take the max intensity in dB (impulse defined as 120 dB at the source), and normalize by 128. Splits are 59 train / 11 val / 15 test maps, with 5,000 samples per train map and 500 per val/test map.

Image encoder: pretrained ResNet-18 on the 360° RGB panorama (4 views of 256x256, 90° FoV) or a 90° ego view toward the listener, followed by adaptive average pooling and normalization, giving a 512-d feature.
Direction-distance encoder: a linear projection of the listener's relative polar coordinates (r, θ) to 16-d.

Predictor: the 528-d concatenation passes through 4 blocks (Linear+BatchNorm+GELU) with shrinking widths 528/256/64/8, giving a scalar regression output or m-binned logits; trained with Huber loss (δ=0.1) and AdamW (lr 0.01, 0.95 decay every 10 epochs).
Action acoustics: record the max dB of robot actions (Stretch fast forward, Go2 running) and scale the predicted normalized max dB RIR by the source loudness to estimate dB at the listener.

ANAVI planning framework: cache panoramas at graph nodes and run ANP per node for known listeners; an LLM or heuristic sets the weight between noise and time-to-go costs; A* plans over slow/normal/fast velocity actions with their audio and time costs.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 (ImageNet-pretrained) + MLP predictor, fine-tuned/trained on simulated data
setting.training_data: Simulated: 59 Matterport3D maps x 5,000 samples (~295k) of panorama + listener polar coordinates + max dB of SoundSpaces 2.0 RIR
setting.observation: 360° RGB panorama at the robot location (4x 256x256 views) + relative polar coordinates of the listener
setting.action_space: Discrete slow/normal/fast motion actions on a graph with A* planning (real path teleoperated on Unitree Go2)
setting.privileged: Listener location is known; the simulator uses mesh and material info only to generate training labels, not at test time. The real-world path demo was teleoperated along a hand-chosen quiet path.

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark is used. The simulation results are given only as plots (distribution coverage and epsilon-accuracy curves) with no tabulated values. The only table gives real-world dB predictions vs. measurements for a few positions (e.g. Stretch 5m W: real 47 dB, predicted 40.28).
results: In simulation on 7,500 test samples, the panoramic ANP (Pano-VisDirDis) gives the best epsilon-thresholded accuracy and distribution coverage versus Heuristic, DisLinReg and DirDisMLP, and is better than the ego-view variant (shown in plots only). In a real bedroom, predictions are within 0.32-3.36 dB at 0.5-1 m but off by 6.72 dB (Stretch) at 5 m. A teleoperated Go2 demo shows a 46 s quieter path versus a 32 s shortest path that passes close to the listener.
limitations: Severe sim-to-real gap: the model mostly learns distance dependence and does not consistently capture walls or corridors in real panoramas, and real errors grow with distance.

Real-world validation is small and qualitative: audio is played back from a laptop speaker, the source gain is guessed (20 dB), and the planning demo is a single teleoperated path with no closed-loop quantitative evaluation.
Only max dB of the impulse response is modeled, with no frequency, duration, ambient noise or listener subjectivity; simulation mesh holes also degrade ray tracing.
